# Education in Nigeria
Education in Nigeria begins with six years of primary schooling, starting at around age five and culminating in a first school-leaving certificate. The curriculum covers mathematics, English, religious knowledge, agricultural science, home economics, and indigenous languages, with private schools offering additional subjects. Following the Universal Primary Education program of 1976, the sector evolved into the Universal Basic Education (UBE) scheme in 1999, mandating nine years of free and compulsory schooling—six years of primary and three years of junior secondary education. The UBE is overseen by the Universal Basic Education Commission (UBEC) and emphasizes continuous assessment, automatic promotion, and access for special populations such as nomads, migrants, girls, and disabled learners.
Secondary education comprises three years of junior and three years of senior secondary school, covering core and elective subjects with vocational tracks. Students undergo promotional examinations, most notably the Senior Secondary Certificate Examination (SSCE), administered by WAEC and NECO, determining university eligibility. Secondary schools are run by federal, state, and private institutions; federal schools are considered elite due to their merit-based admission, while private schools, though costly, generally offer better facilities. Teacher qualifications vary across school types, with federal schools requiring higher certification. Vocational and technical education is available, managed by the National Board for Technical Education and National Business and Technical Examinations Board.
Tertiary education is provided by a mix of federal, state, and private universities, polytechnics, monotechnics, and colleges of education. Admission to universities is generally through SSCE and JAMB exams, with advanced level programs like IJMB and JUPEB facilitating direct entry. Despite expansion, the literacy rate remains low, complicated by regional disparities and challenges such as out-of-school children, teacher shortages, and insufficient infrastructure, especially in rural areas. Government and international efforts aim at improving literacy, female education, and digital skills, but obstacles include poverty, insecurity, gender bias, and underfunding. The sector also features vibrant informal education and adult literacy programs, with ongoing reforms and policies intended to address foundational and systemic gaps in access and quality.
